Intemperance means a lack of self-control or moderation, particularly when it comes to desires, appetites, or behavior. It describes the habit of going too far — of consuming, doing, or expressing something in a way that exceeds reasonable, healthy limits.

Think of it this way: imagine a dial that goes from "too little" to "just right" to "too much." Intemperance is when someone is permanently stuck at "too much" — and doesn't seem to be able or willing to pull it back.
The Most Classic Use: Alcohol

Historically, and still very commonly today, intemperance is most closely associated with the excessive drinking of alcohol. For centuries, the opposite word — temperance — was the name of a whole social movement that urged people to drink less or not at all. So when someone says a person "is given to intemperance," they almost certainly mean that person drinks heavily and without control. This is the word's heartland.
The Broader Meaning

But intemperance is not limited to drinking. It applies to any area of life where someone chronically overindulges or loses restraint:

  • Food: Eating to the point of consistent excess, without knowing when to stop.
  • Emotions: Expressing anger, passion, or grief in a way that is wild and uncontrolled — far beyond what the situation calls for.
  • Speech: Saying harsh, reckless, or offensive things because one lacks the self-discipline to hold back.
  • Spending or pleasure-seeking: Throwing yourself into luxury, sensual pleasure, or entertainment with no sense of limit.

In all these cases, the word points to the same problem: the failure of self-restraint.
It Describes a Pattern, Not Just One Moment

This is important. Intemperance is not what you call a single bad night or one impulsive choice. It refers to a habitual tendency — a recurring, established pattern of excess. If someone occasionally has too much to drink at a party, that's not intemperance. If someone routinely drinks without control and can't seem to stop themselves, that is intemperance.
The Moral Weight It Carries

The word carries a moral and judgmental tone. When you call someone's behavior "intemperance," you are criticizing their character — specifically their willpower, self-discipline, and judgment. It implies that they should be able to control themselves, but are failing to do so. It's not a neutral, clinical word. It's a word of disapproval.

This is why you'll encounter it often in formal writing, moral philosophy, religious texts, literature, and older or elevated speech. In casual modern conversation, people are more likely to say someone "has no self-control" or "goes overboard" — but in more formal or literary contexts, intemperance carries that same idea with far more weight and precision.
Examples in Sentences

• "His intemperance at the dinner table was an embarrassment to his family — he ate and drank as if there were no tomorrow."
  • "The senator's speech was full of intemperance; he insulted his opponents in ways that shocked even his own supporters."
  • "She worried that her husband's intemperance would one day ruin his health."
  • "The philosopher warned that intemperance of any kind — whether in food, wine, or emotion — weakens the mind and the soul."
The Adjective Form: Intemperate

Since you'll often see this family of words together, it helps to know:

Intemperate (adjective) means the same idea applied as a describing word.

  • An intemperate person = someone who lacks self-control.
  • An intemperate remark = a comment that was harsh, reckless, or excessive — one the speaker should have had the self-discipline to withhold or soften.
  • An intemperate climate (a less common use) = weather that is harsh and extreme.
The Opposite: Temperance

The direct antonym of intemperance is temperance, which means moderation, self-restraint, and the discipline to know your limits and respect them. A person of temperance doesn't deny themselves all pleasure — they simply don't let pleasure control them. Intemperance is what happens when that inner brake fails.
Synonyms to Expand Your Understanding

These words overlap with intemperance in different ways:

  • Excess — doing or having too much of something.
  • Overindulgence — giving in too freely to one's desires.
  • Dissipation — wasting oneself through excessive pleasure-seeking (slightly stronger, suggests moral ruin).
  • Immoderation — the absence of moderation; more neutral and less emotional than intemperance.
  • Self-indulgence — prioritizing your own pleasures without restraint.
The One-Line Summary

If you had to carry just one idea with you: intemperance is the habitual failure to control your desires or behavior — the inability or refusal to know when enough is enough. It's not just excess; it's excess that has become a pattern, and a pattern that earns moral criticism.
